title: Lecture 3: Genericity and Information Hiding
summary: This lecture explores generic programming techniques for creating reusable components and information hiding principles for managing complexity and ensuring proper encapsulation in large systems. Students will learn how to design flexible, maintainable software through type parameters, constrained genericity, access control, and interface-implementation separation.
learningObjectives: Understand and apply generic programming concepts to create reusable software components
Design and implement generic classes with appropriate type parameters and constraints
Apply information hiding principles to manage complexity in large-scale systems
Implement proper access control and visibility mechanisms for encapsulation
Distinguish between interface and implementation, designing clean separation boundaries
Build reusable library components following best practices in object-oriented design

sections.title: Introduction to Genericity and Reusability
learningGoals: Understand the motivation for generic programming
Recognize code duplication problems that genericity solves
Appreciate the role of genericity in building reusable components

subsections.title: The Problem: Code Duplication Without Genericity
keyPoints: Traditional approach requires separate implementations for each type (IntStack, StringStack, PersonStack)
Code duplication leads to maintenance nightmares and increased error potential
Type-specific implementations violate the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle
Need for a unified approach to handle multiple types with same logic
examples: Stack implementations for different types showing identical logic
List classes duplicated across Integer, String, and custom object types
Sorting algorithms rewritten for each data type
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Side-by-side comparison of IntStack and StringStack classes showing duplicated code structure

subsections.title: The Solution: Generic Programming
keyPoints: Genericity allows writing code that works with multiple types
Type parameters serve as placeholders for actual types
Single implementation can be instantiated for different types
Enhances code reusability, maintainability, and type safety
examples: Generic Stack<G> replacing multiple type-specific stack implementations
Generic List<T> used with different element types
Generic sorting method working with any comparable type
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Conceptual diagram showing generic class Stack<G> with multiple instantiations (Stack<Integer>, Stack<String>, Stack<Person>)

exercises: Identify code duplication in a set of type-specific collection classes
Sketch a generic version of a simple container class

sections.title: Generic Classes and Type Parameters
learningGoals: Master the syntax and semantics of generic class declarations
Understand type parameter naming conventions and best practices
Learn how to instantiate generic classes with concrete types

subsections.title: Declaring Generic Classes
keyPoints: Syntax: class ClassName<TypeParameter> with type parameters in angle brackets
Type parameters are formal placeholders used throughout the class definition
Convention: single uppercase letters (T, E, K, V, G) or descriptive names
Type parameters can be used for fields, method parameters, and return types
examples: class Stack<G> with push(item: G) and pop: G methods
class Pair<K, V> representing key-value pairs with multiple type parameters
class Box<T> with methods to store and retrieve items of type T
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Anatomy of a generic class declaration showing type parameter placement and usage in method signatures

subsections.title: Type Instantiation and Usage
keyPoints: Creating instances by providing actual type arguments: new Stack<Integer>
Type inference in modern languages can reduce verbosity
Type parameters ensure compile-time type safety
Different instantiations create logically distinct types
examples: stack_of_integers: Stack<Integer> := create {Stack<Integer>}.make
names: List<String> := create {List<String>}.make
Type inference example: var numbers = new ArrayList<Integer>() vs new ArrayList<>()
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Flow diagram showing generic class definition → type instantiation → concrete object creation

exercises: Implement a generic Pair<F, S> class with first and second elements
Create multiple instantiations of a generic Queue class with different types

sections.title: Constrained Genericity
learningGoals: Understand the need for type constraints in generic programming
Apply bounded type parameters to ensure required capabilities
Design generic algorithms with appropriate type constraints

subsections.title: The Need for Constraints
keyPoints: Unconstrained type parameters limit what operations can be performed
Cannot assume any operations beyond those available on Object/ANY
Constraints specify required interfaces or base classes for type arguments
Enable generic code to call specific methods on type parameter instances
examples: Cannot compare elements in generic sort without Comparable constraint
Cannot perform arithmetic on generic type T without numeric constraint
Need for constraint when implementing generic max/min functions
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison showing unconstrained generic class with limited operations vs constrained generic with expanded capabilities

subsections.title: Implementing Type Constraints
keyPoints: Syntax varies by language: <T extends Comparable> in Java, {G -> COMPARABLE} in Eiffel
Constraints can specify interfaces, base classes, or multiple bounds
Type arguments must satisfy all specified constraints
Constraints enable calling methods defined in the constraint type
examples: class SortedList<G -> COMPARABLE> ensuring elements can be compared
class NumericProcessor<T extends Number> for numeric operations
class Repository<E extends Entity & Serializable> with multiple constraints
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML-style diagram showing generic class with constraint relationship to interface/base class

subsections.title: Designing with Constraints
keyPoints: Choose minimal necessary constraints for maximum reusability
Overly restrictive constraints limit applicability of generic code
Design interfaces specifically for use as generic constraints
Balance between flexibility and required functionality
examples: Comparable interface designed for sorting algorithms
Hashable interface for hash-based collections
Cloneable interface for generic copy operations
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Decision tree for selecting appropriate type constraints based on required operations

exercises: Implement a generic findMax method with appropriate constraints
Design a generic binary search tree with constrained type parameter
Refactor unconstrained generic code to add necessary constraints

sections.title: Information Hiding Principles
learningGoals: Understand the fundamental principles of information hiding
Recognize the benefits of hiding implementation details
Apply information hiding to manage complexity in large systems

subsections.title: Foundations of Information Hiding
keyPoints: Information hiding: concealing design decisions that are likely to change
Parnas's principle: modules should hide design decisions from each other
Reduces coupling between system components
Enables independent evolution of module implementations
examples: Database implementation hidden behind repository interface
Data structure choice (array vs linked list) hidden from clients
Encryption algorithm details hidden in security module
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Layered architecture showing public interfaces hiding private implementation details

subsections.title: Benefits and Trade-offs
keyPoints: Reduces complexity by limiting what clients need to understand
Enables implementation changes without affecting clients
Supports parallel development by different teams
May introduce performance overhead through abstraction layers
examples: Changing from ArrayList to LinkedList without client code changes
Upgrading database system while maintaining same API
Optimizing internal algorithms without breaking existing code
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Before/after comparison showing implementation change with stable interface

exercises: Identify information that should be hidden in a given class design
Analyze a code example for information hiding violations

sections.title: Access Control and Visibility
learningGoals: Master access control mechanisms (private, protected, public)
Apply appropriate visibility levels to class members
Design class interfaces with proper encapsulation

subsections.title: Access Control Levels
keyPoints: Private: accessible only within the class itself
Protected: accessible within class and subclasses (use cautiously)
Public: accessible from anywhere (forms the class interface)
Package/internal: accessible within same package/assembly (language-dependent)
examples: Private fields with public getter/setter methods
Protected helper methods for subclass extension
Public API methods forming the contract with clients
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Concentric circles showing visibility scopes from private (innermost) to public (outermost)

subsections.title: Designing Class Interfaces
keyPoints: Default to private, expose only what's necessary
Public interface should be minimal and stable
Implementation details should always be private
Use properties/accessors instead of direct field access
examples: BankAccount class with private balance field and public deposit/withdraw methods
Collection class hiding internal array with public add/remove/size methods
Configuration class with private validation logic
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Class diagram showing clear separation between public interface (above line) and private implementation (below line)

exercises: Review a class and assign appropriate access levels to all members
Refactor a class with public fields to use proper encapsulation

sections.title: Interface vs. Implementation Separation
learningGoals: Understand the distinction between interface and implementation
Design clean interfaces independent of implementation
Apply the Dependency Inversion Principle

subsections.title: Interface as Contract
keyPoints: Interface defines what a component does, not how it does it
Specifies method signatures, preconditions, postconditions, invariants
Forms a contract between provider and client
Should be stable while implementation can evolve
examples: List interface with add, remove, get operations independent of array/linked implementation
PaymentProcessor interface hiding specific payment gateway details
Logger interface abstracting over file/database/network logging
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Interface-implementation relationship showing multiple implementations of same interface

subsections.title: Programming to Interfaces
keyPoints: Depend on abstractions (interfaces) not concrete implementations
Enables substitutability and flexibility
Facilitates testing through mock implementations
Supports plugin architectures and extensibility
examples: Declaring variables as List<T> rather than ArrayList<T>
Dependency injection using interface types
Strategy pattern with interchangeable algorithm implementations
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Dependency diagram showing client depending on interface, with multiple concrete implementations

subsections.title: Design by Contract in Interfaces
keyPoints: Preconditions: what must be true before method execution
Postconditions: what must be true after method execution
Class invariants: properties that always hold
Contracts are part of the interface, not implementation
examples: Stack.pop requires not is_empty (precondition)
BankAccount.withdraw ensures balance updated correctly (postcondition)
Queue invariant: count >= 0
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Method signature with annotated preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants

exercises: Design an interface for a cache system with multiple possible implementations
Write contracts (preconditions/postconditions) for a queue interface
Refactor code to depend on interfaces rather than concrete classes

sections.title: Building Reusable Library Components
learningGoals: Apply genericity and information hiding to create reusable libraries
Design components with broad applicability
Follow best practices for library design

subsections.title: Principles of Reusable Design
keyPoints: Generality: solve broader problem class, not just specific case
Simplicity: minimal interface with maximum functionality
Consistency: follow established patterns and conventions
Completeness: provide all necessary operations for the abstraction
examples: Generic collection library (List, Set, Map) usable across domains
Utility library with broadly applicable algorithms (sort, search, filter)
Logging framework adaptable to different output targets
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Reusability pyramid showing layers from specific solutions to general libraries

subsections.title: Library Design Best Practices
keyPoints: Minimize dependencies on external libraries
Provide clear, comprehensive documentation
Design for extension through inheritance or composition
Version interfaces carefully to maintain backward compatibility
examples: Java Collections Framework as exemplar of reusable library design
Apache Commons libraries providing general-purpose utilities
Standard Template Library (STL) in C++ with generic algorithms
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Component diagram showing well-designed library with minimal external dependencies

subsections.title: Combining Genericity and Information Hiding
keyPoints: Use genericity for type flexibility while hiding implementation
Generic interfaces with multiple concrete implementations
Type parameters enable reuse across different data types
Information hiding allows implementation optimization without API changes
examples: Generic HashMap<K,V> hiding hash table implementation details
Generic repository pattern with interface and multiple storage backends
Generic event system with type-safe event handlers
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Architecture diagram showing generic interface layer above multiple hidden implementations

exercises: Design a generic, reusable caching library with proper information hiding
Implement a generic priority queue with hidden heap implementation
Create a generic observer pattern implementation for event handling

sections.title: Practical Applications and Case Studies
learningGoals: Analyze real-world applications of genericity and information hiding
Evaluate design decisions in existing libraries
Apply learned principles to solve practical problems

subsections.title: Case Study: Collection Frameworks
keyPoints: Generic type parameters for element types (List<E>, Map<K,V>)
Interface hierarchy hiding implementation diversity
Constrained genericity for comparable/hashable elements
Information hiding in internal data structure choices
examples: Java Collections Framework architecture
Eiffel EiffelBase library structure
C# generic collections in System.Collections.Generic
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram of collection framework showing interfaces and implementations

subsections.title: Design Patterns with Genericity
keyPoints: Factory pattern with generic product types
Repository pattern with generic entity types
Observer pattern with generic event types
Strategy pattern with generic context types
examples: Generic Factory<T> creating instances of type T
Repository<TEntity> for data access abstraction
Observable<T> for type-safe event notifications
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Pattern structure diagram showing generic type parameters in pattern participants

exercises: Analyze the design of a standard library (Java Collections, .NET generics, etc.)
Implement a design pattern using generics and information hiding
Critique a library design for proper use of genericity and encapsulation

sections.title: Summary and Integration
learningGoals: Synthesize concepts of genericity and information hiding
Connect to broader software engineering principles
Prepare for applying concepts in software construction projects

subsections.title: Key Takeaways
keyPoints: Genericity enables type-safe code reuse across different types
Constrained genericity balances flexibility with required functionality
Information hiding manages complexity by concealing implementation details
Interface-implementation separation enables evolution and substitutability
Combining these principles creates robust, reusable library components
examples: Well-designed generic library component exemplifying all principles
Comparison of poor vs. excellent application of these concepts
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Concept map showing relationships between genericity, information hiding, encapsulation, and reusability

subsections.title: Connection to Software Quality Attributes
keyPoints: Reusability: genericity enables use across contexts
Maintainability: information hiding localizes changes
Extensibility: interface separation supports extension
Correctness: type safety and contracts ensure reliability
examples: How these principles support the quality goals from module ILOs
Trade-offs between different quality attributes
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Quality attribute tree showing how genericity and information hiding contribute to overall software quality

Prepare for tutorial exercises on generic programming and encapsulation
